title: TB5-10731
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, appeals a decision by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection, he has not submitted new evidence in support of his claim and he has not requested an oral hearing.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Pakistan, appeals a decision by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection, he has not submitted new evidence in support of his claim and he has not requested an oral hearing. The Appellant requests that the determination of the RPD be set aside and his claim be allowed by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). Alternatively the Appellant requests that the RAD remit the matter to the RPD for reconsideration by a differently-constituted panel.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Division (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed.
The Appellant alleged he is a Shia Muslim who served as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and was active in his religious community.
He left Pakistan in 2009 because he feared his life was at risk from his brothers as a result of conflict over his father's estate.
He travelled to the United Kingdom (UK) on a study visa on XXXX XXXX, 2009, and attended a school until 2011 when the school closed. His study visa expired on XXXX XXXX, 2012.
He returned to Pakistan for a visit in XXXX 2011 for approximately a month and a half, and his problems with his brothers were resolved.
He made an unsuccessful refugee claim in the UK in XXXX 2012, and he was deported to Pakistan in XXXX 2014.
In Pakistan he resumed his activities in support of the local Imam XXXX and started receiving threatening calls from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2014.

He was assaulted on XXXX XXXX, 2014 and told he would be killed if he continued to ignore the XXXX demand to stop his community activities. Threats were made to his family as well even after he came to Canada.
He fears the XXXX and states that protection from the police is not available and there is no internal flight alternative available to him. The Issues
The RPD panel indicates that the determinative issue in this claim is credibility.

The Appellant submits the issues in this appeal are: * What is the appropriate standard of review? * Did the RPD err in its credibility findings, including the credibility of documentary evidence adduced in support of the claim? The Role of the RAD
While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.
The RAD now has the benefit of Federal Court jurisprudence which speaks to the appellate tribunal's role in relation to that of the RPD.

In this regard, the Court in Huruglica considered the appropriate relationship between the RAD and the RPD.1 In Huruglica, the Court determined that the RAD is to conduct a "hybrid appeal." It is to review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of the Appellant's refugee claim, deferring to the RPD only where the lower tribunal enjoys a particular advantage in reaching a conclusion. Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own determination.

The Court determined that, in conducting its assessment, the RAD can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion. The RAD is, however, not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on the facts only where there is "palpable and overriding error."
The RAD will review all of the evidence in the RPD record and come to its own independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
The RAD notes the Appellant submits a brief analysis of his view of the appropriate standard of review which reflects the RAD's view as stated above. Credibility Religious observance in the UK

The panel noted the Appellant stated he was at risk in Pakistan because of his religious activities. The panel questioned the Appellant as to his religious activities in the UK from 2009 to 2014. The Appellant responded he went to the mosque for Friday prayers whenever he had time. He further stated he went four times a month.

The panel noted the Appellant testified that he pinned to serve his religious community during his four and a half years in the UK, but he was unable to spare the time. He was deported in 2014 and thought his problems in the UK resulted from his lack of service to his religion and the community. The Appellant further testified he went to the majlis only once in two months.

The panel asked the Appellant if he had any corroborating evidence of his UK religious observance such as a letter from the Imam XXXX, a photograph or a receipt. The Appellant responded he did not do anything there and donations were made by his wife in Pakistan.

The panel drew a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility with regards to the lack of involvement in religious activities in the UK seemed inconsistent with his alleged activities in Pakistan.

The Appellant submits his lack of involvement in religious activity in the UK does not inherently indicate his stated religious activism in Pakistan lacks credibility. The Appellant further submits he explained he had difficulty sparing enough time for community service while working and studying in the UK. The Appellant notes his testimony was consistent with his BOC narrative.
The Appellant submits that the panel's finding that his testimony concerning his account of his religious activities in the UK seemed to evolve was unsubstantiated and unreasonable.
The Appellant also submits the panel's requirement of objective corroboration concerning his religious activities in the UK, given his admittedly low level of involvement, was unreasonable.
The Appellant submits the panel's negative credibility inference concerning his lack of involvement in the UK Shia community is unreasonable in light of the circumstances noted above.

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence in the RPD record concerning the Appellant's religious activities in the UK. The RAD notes the panel made no specific findings concerning the lack of corroborating documentation and the Appellant's evolving testimony in this regard. The RAD finds, in the context of the Appellant's evidence concerning his commitment to Shia Islam and his alleged religious activities in Pakistan, that the Appellant's lack of any substantive religious activity for approximately four and a half years in the UK raises a doubt concerning his evidence about his commitment to Shia Islam and the Shia community. The RAD concurs with the panel's finding in this regard. Misrepresentation regarding his UK student visa

The panel noted a UK Home Office document2 that suggested he submitted false documents indicating he was still attending school when this was not the case, and seeking an extension of his study visa. The Appellant explained he contacted a lawyer regarding an extension of his visa, and false documentation was attached to the application. The Appellant further explained that he was not informed about the use of false documentation. He stated as well he was aware this was a criminal act but he took no responsibility and he was surprised when he was informed about this by UK immigration officials.

The panel indicated that the Appellant was the only party benefiting from the false documentation and found that it did not believe the Appellant was unaware of the use of documentation indicating he was still enrolled in school when he was not. The panel drew a negative inference in this regard.

The Appellant submits the panel's finding in this regard is unreasonable. The Appellant notes his dependence on a Pakistani lawyer and the misrepresentations do not go to the heart of his claim in Canada which concerns incidents of religious persecution in Pakistan and not in the UK. The Appellant further submits the misrepresentations were not necessarily determinative of the credibility of such material incidents.

The RAD has reviewed the evidence in the RPD record concerning the Appellant's UK visa and the Appellant's misrepresentations. The RAD agrees the incidents in the UK do not go to the core of the Appellant's refugee claim in Canada. The RAD finds however that the Appellant's misrepresentations in the UK do raise a doubt about his general credibility. The RAD further finds in this regard that the Appellant's testimony that he was unaware of the fraudulent nature of documentation attached to the extension application strains credulity as he was making an application for the extension of his student visa when he knew he was no longer studying in a college. Discrepancies arising from UK Home Office documentation

The panel noted that in a form he filed with the UK government3 he indicated he was single and without children when this was not the case. The Appellant explained a consultant advised him he would be denied a visa if he indicated he was married. He noted he had been denied a visa twice in the past and he feared another rejection. The Appellant further stated the consultant misguided him but he noted he had no other option as he was in danger.

The panel indicated the Appellant's testimony indicates he was willing to say whatever suited his convenience when dealing with immigration authorities. The panel noted in the hearing that the Appellant's lawyer in the UK indicated the Appellant has been the subject of torture and can be a victim again. The Appellant was asked what this referred to and he responded "I am not sure." Subsequently he testified he had been beaten by his brothers during a visit to Pakistan in 2011.

The panel noted there was no mention of torture in the Appellant's Basis of Claim Form (BOC) and drew a negative inference form the Appellant's inability to provide consistent and coherent information in this regard.

The panel asked the Appellant why he did not mention he was beaten by his brothers in 2011. The Appellant responded he told his counsel's interpreter that he was beaten many times, he was detained a few times in the UK and he was under a lot of stress at the time. He further testified his beating in Pakistan and mistreatment in England slipped his mind when writing his BOC narrative.
The panel indicated, in the absence of any medical documentation explaining the Appellant's forgetfulness, it drew a negative inference from these omissions.
The RAD notes the Appellant makes no submission in this regard. Overstay in the UK

The panel noted the Appellant's study visa expired on XXXX XXXX, 2012, although it was arguable his student status expired in 2011 when the school closed. The panel further noted the Appellant remained in the UK working illegally until he was arrested and then made a refugee claim in XXXX 2012, alleging he was at risk from his brothers.

The panel noted the Appellant made his claim for protection only after his arrest. The panel further noted the Appellant's willingness to remain illegally in the UK and at risk of deportation negatively impacts on his credibility and shows a lack of subjective fear.

The Appellant submits the panel's finding in this regard does not reasonably lead to its adverse finding regarding the credibility of his evidence concerning incidents of persecution in Pakistan. The Appellant further submits his overstay in the UK did not reasonably lead to a lack of subjective fear regarding the incidents of persecution. The Appellant notes the panel failed to distinguish between the incidents and circumstances that prompted the Appellant to go to the UK and those that prompted him to come to Canada.

The RAD agrees with the Appellant that his overstay in the UK does not reasonably lead to an adverse finding regarding the credibility of his evidence concerning incidents of persecution in Pakistan that resulted in his making a claim for protection in Canada. The RAD finds however that the Appellant's actions in this regard in the UK does raise a further doubt about his general credibility. The letters from the Imam XXXX

The panel noted the Appellant corroborated his fear of the XXXX with a XXXX XXXX, 2015 letter4 allegedly written by a person who described himself as the president of the Imam XXXX. The letter indicated the Appellant faced threats from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX due to his conversion to the Shia faith. The panel noted the Appellant claimed to be a Shia from birth, and that it was the XXXX and not XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who is the agent of persecution. When the Appellant was made aware of the inconsistencies he had his brother seek a replacement letter5 which was mailed on XXXX XXXX, 2015. The Appellant explained the letter writer indicated that he had written the letter for someone else but sent it to the Appellant by mistake.
The panel noted the second letter indicated that the letter writer explained the errors were due to "a typo mistake on my part."

The panel noted in the hearing that the initial letter was accurate in many respects as it named the Appellant, indicated he served as general secretary of the Imam XXXX in 2009 and noted the beatings and threats. The Appellant was asked why the initial letter noted he was a convert to Shia Islam. The Appellant explained the letter was written for someone else. The Appellant was asked why a mistake was made in regard to the agent of persecution. The Appellant responded he did not know and noted the letter writer had indicated he made a mistake. Subsequently the Appellant stated he called the letter writer and he said this happened to someone else and he cut and pasted.

The panel noted the Appellant explained the discrepancies in the first letter were the result of the letter having been written for someone else. The panel further noted that this was not what the letter writer said in the second letter in which it was indicated the discrepancies were "a typo mistake on my part."6

The panel noted the Appellant's explanations for the discrepancy seemed to evolve, no explanation was provided as to why much of the initial letter apparently was accurate and the explanation of a typographical error is not persuasive regarding the issues of conversion and the agent of persecution.

The panel found the two letters are completely unreliable, and possibly fraudulent, and it accorded them no weight. In addition the panel drew a negative inference in this regard as to the Appellant's credibility.

The Appellant submits the panel's negative credibility inference in this regard is unreasonable. The Appellant further submits the letter writer provided a reasonable explanation for the errors in the original letter. The Appellant further submits the panel's use of the phrase "...the panel again and I hate and lovely day is that okay into..." are somewhat ambiguous and/or unintelligible and as such casts doubt on the reliability of its findings."7

The RAD has reviewed all of the evidence in the RPD record concerning these two letters and the Appellant's testimony in this regard. The RAD is not persuaded that the letter writer provided a reasonable explanation for the errors in the original letter. The RAD finds the panel did not err in its findings concerning the letters and the explanations for the discrepancy. The RAD agrees with the panel's analysis in this regard.

The RAD agrees with the Appellant as to the ambiguity and/or unintelligible nature of the panel's phrase cited above. The RAD finds however that this phrase reflects poor proof reading by the panel and it does not cast doubt on the reliability of its findings in this regard. The availability of false documentation in Pakistan
The panel noted the Appellant provided a medical report dated XXXX XXXX, 2014, allegedly pertaining to injuries received in a beating.8

The panel further noted the Appellant testified that his mother was able to get a doctor to misrepresent that she had a XXXX XXXX to assist her restoring peace among her sons. The Appellant acknowledged his mother's medical document was fraudulent. The panel noted as well the ease in obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan.9 The panel also noted the Appellant did not explain why his medical document should be considered authentic when his mother's document was not.

The Appellant submits the ease in obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan does not necessarily render his medical report inauthentic. The Appellant further submits the fraudulent nature of his mother's medical document does not necessarily indicate his own medical document is fraudulent.
The Appellant submits as well the panel failed to make a definitive finding as to the authenticity of the report pertaining to the Appellant as it was required to do and this is a reviewable error.

The RAD agrees with the Appellant that the ease in obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan and the fraudulent nature of the Appellant's mother's medical document does not necessarily mean the Appellant's medical document is fraudulent. The RAD further agrees with the Appellant that the panel does not make a definitive finding regarding the authenticity or fraudulent nature of his medical document.

The RAD has reviewed the medical document disclosed by the Appellant.10 The RAD notes this document indicates under the title "Description of Injuries" the words "History of Assault" followed by a list of injuries. The RAD further notes there is no evidence in this document as to the perpetrators of the assault or the reasons for it. The RAD gives this document little evidentiary weight as to the central issue in this appeal. The panel's conclusion

The panel found, on the basis of credibility findings noted above, that the Appellant was not a credible witness. The panel further found the Appellant's allegations that he was attacked and threatened and faces risks in Pakistan are not true. The panel concluded that the Appellant has not provided sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to allow a positive determination of his claim.
The Appellant submits that the panel did not provide good or valid reasons for effectively finding that the presumption of truthfulness to which he is entitled has been rebutted.

The RAD disagrees. The RAD has reviewed the totality of the evidence in the RPD record and, as noted above, finds the Appellant's record of untruthfulness and his delay in making a claim for protection in the UK until he was arrested raises a doubt as to his general credibility. The RAD further finds that the Appellant's disclosure of two letters that are likely fraudulent and the discrepancy in his explanation from that provided by the letter writer is sufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness regarding his allegations.
The RAD agrees with the panel that the Appellant has failed to provide sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to allow a positive decision in regard to his claim. Disposition

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA , the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed.
